newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government says committed to federalism.
newsitem.headline: Italian government says committed to federalism.

text.p: Italy's government pledged to press on with federal reform on Monday, acknowledging that separatist Umberto Bossi remained a threat to unity despite his failure to draw mass support for a weekend "declaration of independence".

"The fact that the Northern League flopped doesn't mean that the need for reform has become any less urgent," Regional Affairs Minister Franco Bassanini told a news conference a day after Bossi's symbolic proclamation of a northern "republic".
He said Bossi's League had drawn fewer than 150,000 people to its pro-secession rallies in the north while more than one million Italians demonstrated nationwide in favour of unity.
But Bassanini said the centre-left government of Prime Minister Romano Prodi would forge ahead with projects aimed at constitutional reform and eventual federalism.

Unless Italy enacted institutional reforms aimed at more local autonomy and a streamlined bureaucracy there was "a risk that a separatist programme would be embraced out of desperation by those who really don't want it," Bassanini said.
"The road ahead is that of federalist reform," he said.
Prodi's government is already working on two packages of laws aimed giving local authorities more say in administrative matters and taxation and to eliminate bureaucratic waste.
A parliamentary commission will have two years to work out constitutional reform aimed at giving Italy a federal structure. After it is approved by the legislature it will have to go to a referendum.
Bassanini said all institutional reforms possible without changing the constitution should be carried out before.
The morning after Bossi formally declared "independence" for his would-be "Padania", commentators said the fundamental grievances of many northerners were still to be resolved.
Many in the industrial north say institutions they perceive as corrupt, a centralised government, and high taxes to fund an incompetent bureaucracy are at the base of their complaints.

Italy's media portrayed as a fiasco Bossi's bid to split the wealthy north away from what he has denounced as the corrupt, Mafia-ridden south but political commentators cautioned that the separatist was far from finished.
"Declaring victory, as some "Italian' politicians will, would be a mistake," said Sergio Romano in a front-page column in the leading northern daily newspaper La Stampa.
"If the opera is a comic one and the leading actor an uncontrollable ham, the gist of the libretto remains nonetheless serious and dramatic," Romano commented.
The Vatican newspaper L'Osservatore Romano called Bossi's declaration of independence "a deep wound and an outrage for the nation" but also warned that it would be "superficial" to write Bossi off.
In declaring independence in Venice on Sunday, Bossi said Padania was "a sovereign and independent federal republic" and announced a temporary constitution and provisional government.
The League also read out a 10-point "Bill of rights for the citizens of Padania" in which the formation of a Padanian national guard was to be set up to defend the state.
Bossi's actions defied a constitutional ban on challenges to the unity of the state and prompted a call from a former constitutional court president, Ettore Gallo, for his arrest.
Bassanini said only magistrates could decide if Bossi had broken the law and if any legal action should be taken. "The government cannot and should not intervene," he said.
